q: The concept of temperature is very important for the physical and biological sciences.
e: Temperature is directly related to the energies of molecules composing the object, making it crucial for these sciences.

q: The temperature of an object is directly related to the energies of molecules composing the object.
e: Temperature serves as an indicator of the internal energy changes within the molecules of an object.

q: Natural processes often involve energy changes and the temperature is an indicator for these changes.
e: Temperature reflects the energy changes that occur during natural processes.

q: Thermal energy is an internal energy of a matter.
e: Thermal energy is indeed the internal energy of matter, resulting from molecular motion and position.

q: Heat is considered to be a form of energy.
e: Heat is defined as the energy exchanged between an object and its surroundings due to temperature differences.

q: Heat and temperature are the same quantities.
e: Heat and temperature are different quantities; heat is energy in transit, while temperature measures hotness or coldness.

q: Temperature is the quantity that determines how cold (or) how hot the object is.
e: Temperature quantitatively expresses the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

q: The temperature of a hot body is lower than that of a cold body.
e: The temperature of a hot body is higher than that of a cold body.

q: To measure temperature accurately, we use instruments called thermometers.
e: Thermometers are the standard instruments designed for accurate temperature measurement.

q: The energy exchanged between an object and its surrounding due to different temperatures is defined as heat.
e: Heat is specifically the energy transferred due to a temperature difference.

q: Heat is the energy in transit.
e: Heat is defined as energy moving from a higher temperature body to a lower temperature body.

q: The unit of heat is different from the units of energy.
e: The unit of heat is the same as the units of energy, such as the joule.

q: When a body at a higher temperature is in contact with a body at a lower temperature, heat flows from the second to the first body.
e: Heat flows from the first body (higher temperature) to the second body (lower temperature).

q: The motions and positions of molecules in matter result in the kinetic energy and potential energy.
e: Molecular motion contributes to kinetic energy, while molecular positions contribute to potential energy.

q: The total energy, that is, the sum of the potential energy and the kinetic energy, of molecules in matter is in fact the external energy of that matter.
e: The sum of the potential and kinetic energy of molecules in matter is the internal energy of that matter.

q: Temperature is a measure of the internal energy of molecules.
e: Temperature is directly related to and measures the internal energy of the molecules in a substance.

q: Every thermometer uses a physical property that varies with temperature.
e: This varying physical property is the fundamental basis for all thermometer operations.

q: This property is referred to as the thermometric property of the thermometer.
e: The specific physical property that changes with temperature is called the thermometric property.

q: The thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the thermal contraction of the liquid.
e: The thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the thermal expansion of the liquid.

q: The liquid-in-glass thermometer consists of a thin glass bulb joined to a capillary tube with a narrow bore which is sealed at its other end.
e: This structural design allows the liquid to expand into the narrow capillary tube for measurement.

q: When the bulb becomes warmer, the liquid in it expands less than the bulb.
e: When the bulb becomes warmer, the liquid in it expands more than the bulb, forcing liquid into the capillary tube.

q: The thinner the bulb wall is, the faster the response of the thermometer will be when the temperature changes.
e: A thinner bulb wall allows for quicker heat transfer, resulting in a faster thermometer response.

q: The liquid used usually contains mercury (or) coloured alcohol.
e: Mercury and coloured alcohol are the standard liquids used in liquid-in-glass thermometers.

q: Alcohol has a higher freezing point than mercury so it is more suitable for low-temperature measurements.
e: Alcohol has a lower freezing point than mercury, making it more suitable for low-temperature measurements.

q: Thermocouple thermometers are electrical thermometers which make use of the voltage that develops when two different metals are in contact.
e: This voltage generation at the junction of two different metals is the principle behind thermocouple thermometers.

q: This voltage varies with pressure.
e: This voltage varies with temperature, not pressure.

q: One of the junctions is maintained at $0^{\circ} ext{C}$ and the other junction is used as the temperature probe.
e: Maintaining a reference junction at $0^{\circ}	ext{C}$ allows the other junction to accurately measure the target temperature.

q: The voltmeter can be calibrated directly in $^{\circ} ext{C}$.
e: The voltmeter measuring the thermocouple's voltage can be directly calibrated to display temperature in $^{\circ}	ext{C}$.

q: Because of the large size of a thermocouple junction, thermocouple thermometers are used to measure rapidly changing temperatures.
e: Because of the small size of a thermocouple junction, they are used to measure rapidly changing temperatures.

q: Thermocouple thermometers can be used to measure much lower temperatures than liquid-in-glass thermometers.
e: Thermocouple thermometers can be used to measure much higher temperatures than liquid-in-glass thermometers.

q: The voltage of a thermocouple can be measured and recorded automatically.
e: The electrical nature of the thermocouple output allows for automatic measurement and recording.

q: Resistance thermometer uses the fact that the electrical resistance of a metal (e.g platinum) wire decreases with temperature.
e: A resistance thermometer uses the fact that the electrical resistance of a metal wire increases with temperature.

q: A resistance thermometer can measure temperatures accurately in the range $-200^{\circ} ext{C}$ to $1200^{\circ} ext{C}$.
e: This wide range makes resistance thermometers highly versatile for accurate temperature measurement.

q: A resistance thermometer is best for rapidly changing temperatures.
e: A resistance thermometer is best for steady temperatures, not rapidly changing ones.

q: A resistance thermometer is small in size.
e: A resistance thermometer is bulky, not small.

q: Thermometric substances can be solids, liquids (or) gases.
e: Any state of matter can serve as a thermometric substance if it has a suitable varying physical property.

q: They have physical properties that vary continuously and linearly with temperature.
e: This continuous and linear variation is essential for accurate and predictable temperature measurement.

q: Temperature units depend on the scale used.
e: Different temperature scales, such as Celsius or Kelvin, dictate the specific units used.

q: The temperature scales most widely used today are Celsius (Centigrade), Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales.
e: These three scales are the standard references for temperature measurement globally.

q: The SI unit of temperature is Celsius ($^{\circ} ext{C}$).
e: The SI unit of temperature is kelvin (K).

q: To calibrate a thermometer, two reference points are chosen and the interval between these points is subdivided into a number of equal parts.
e: This subdivision creates the standardized scale markings on the thermometer.

q: The freezing point and boiling point of water under normal atmospheric pressure are chosen as reference points.
e: These two fixed points of water provide a reliable and reproducible basis for calibration.

q: The interval between these two points is divided into one thousand equal parts for the Celsius scale.
e: The interval between these two points is divided into one hundred equal parts for the Celsius scale.

q: On the Celsius scale, the ice point is $0^{\circ} ext{C}$ and the steam point is $100^{\circ} ext{C}$.
e: These are the standard fixed points defining the Celsius temperature scale.

q: On the Fahrenheit scale the ice point is $0^{\circ} ext{F}$ and the steam point is $212^{\circ} ext{F}$.
e: On the Fahrenheit scale, the ice point is $32^{\circ}	ext{F}$ and the steam point is $212^{\circ}	ext{F}$.

q: On the Kelvin scale the ice point is $273 ext{ K}$ and the steam point is $373 ext{ K}$.
e: These values correspond to the freezing and boiling points of water on the absolute Kelvin scale.

q: The relationship between the Celsius temperature $T_C$ and the Fahrenheit temperature $T_F$ is given by the equation $T_F = 1.8T_C + 32$.
e: This equation accurately converts a temperature value from the Celsius scale to the Fahrenheit scale.

q: The relationship between the Celsius temperature $T_C$ and kelvin temperature $T_K$ is given by $T_C + 273 = T_K$.
e: This equation is used to convert a temperature from the Celsius scale to the Kelvin scale.

q: Normal body temperature is $98.6^{\circ} ext{F}$, which is $37.0^{\circ} ext{C}$ on the Celsius scale.
e: This is the standard conversion for normal human body temperature between the two scales.

q: When a substance is heated, its volume usually increases.
e: Heating a substance typically causes its dimensions and overall volume to increase.

q: The dimensions of the substance increase correspondingly.
e: As volume increases due to heating, the linear dimensions of the substance also increase.

q: This increase in size can be explained in terms of the decreased kinetic energy of the molecules.
e: This increase in size is explained by the increased kinetic energy of the molecules.

q: The additional kinetic energy results in each molecule colliding more forcefully with its neighbours.
e: Higher kinetic energy causes more forceful molecular collisions, pushing molecules further apart.

q: Therefore, the molecules push each other further apart and the substance which is heated increases in size.
e: This molecular separation is the fundamental cause of thermal expansion in substances.

q: Increasing the temperature of a gas at constant pressure causes the volume of the gas to decrease.
e: Increasing the temperature of a gas at constant pressure causes the volume of the gas to increase.

q: This increase occurs not only for gases, but also for liquids and solids.
e: Thermal expansion is a general phenomenon that affects all three states of matter.

q: In general, if the temperature of a substance increases, so does its volume.
e: This direct relationship between temperature and volume is the definition of thermal expansion.

q: This phenomenon is known as thermal contraction.
e: This phenomenon is known as thermal expansion.

q: Concrete roadway segments of a sidewalk are separated by gaps because concrete expands with increasing temperature.
e: These gaps are intentionally designed to accommodate the thermal expansion of the concrete.

q: Without these gaps, thermal expansion would cause the segments to push against each other, and they would eventually buckle and break apart.
e: The gaps prevent structural damage by providing space for the concrete to expand into.

q: Although two different metal bars of the same length are heated such that the increase in temperature is the same, the magnitudes of their expansion may not be the same.
e: Different materials have different coefficients of linear expansion, leading to different expansion magnitudes.

q: The expansion of copper is one and a half times that of steel.
e: Copper has a higher coefficient of linear expansion than steel, causing it to expand more under the same conditions.

q: Aluminium expands twice as much as steel does.
e: Aluminium has a significantly higher coefficient of linear expansion compared to steel.

q: The dependence of the change in length of an object on its original length and change in temperature is $\Delta l = \alpha l \Delta T$.
e: This is the standard mathematical formula for calculating linear thermal expansion.

q: In the equation $\Delta l = \alpha l \Delta T$, $\alpha$ is the coefficient of volume expansion.
e: In this equation, $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion.

q: The coefficient of linear expansion is the change in length per unit length for one degree change in temperature.
e: This is the precise definition of the coefficient of linear expansion.

q: The unit of $\alpha$ is per K, which can be written as $ ext{K}^{-1}$.
e: Since it represents change per unit length per degree, the unit simplifies to inverse kelvin.

q: The coefficient of linear expansion for steel is $1.27 imes 10^{-5} ext{ K}^{-1}$.
e: This is the standard accepted value for the linear expansion coefficient of steel as provided in the text.

q: The relations analogous to the one which gives the increase in length $\Delta l$ for the increase in temperature $\Delta T$ can be derived for the area expansion and volume expansion.
e: Similar mathematical relationships exist for two-dimensional area and three-dimensional volume expansion.

q: The relation for area expansion is $\Delta A =  eta A \Delta T$.
e: This formula calculates the change in area due to a change in temperature.

q: The relation for volume expansion is $\Delta V = \gamma V \Delta T$.
e: This formula calculates the change in volume due to a change in temperature.

q: In these equations, $ eta$ is the coefficient of volume expansion and $\gamma$ is the coefficient of area expansion.
e: In these equations, $ eta$ is the coefficient of area expansion and $\gamma$ is the coefficient of volume expansion.

q: The coefficient of area expansion of a substance is the change in area per unit area for one degree change in temperature.
e: This is the exact definition of the coefficient of area expansion.

q: The coefficient of volume expansion of a substance is the change in volume per unit volume for one degree change in temperature.
e: This is the exact definition of the coefficient of volume expansion.

q: Generally all substances expand on heating and contract on cooling.
e: This is the standard behavior for the vast majority of substances.

q: But in the case of water the behavior is different, when water at $0^{\circ} ext{C}$ is heated its volume decreases up to $4^{\circ} ext{C}$ and density increases.
e: Water exhibits unique behavior in this temperature range, contracting instead of expanding.

q: At $4^{\circ} ext{C}$ the density becomes minimum and beyond this temperature volume start to increase.
e: At $4^{\circ}	ext{C}$ the density of water becomes maximum, not minimum.

q: This unusual expansion of water is called anomalous expansion of water.
e: The term 'anomalous expansion' specifically describes water's unique density behavior between $0^{\circ}	ext{C}$ and $4^{\circ}	ext{C}$.
